title: Rotate Image
directAnswer: Rotate an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place. The cheap-but-wasteful answer copies into a second matrix with the mapping new[j][n−1−i] = old[i][j]. The interview answer uses the identity 90° clockwise = transpose, then reverse each row — both done in place for O(1) extra space.

remember.pattern: In-place matrix rotation via transpose + row reversal
remember.formula:
transpose:  for i in 0..n: for j in i+1..n: swap(M[i][j], M[j][i])
reverse each row:  for each row: row.reverse()
# 90° clockwise = transpose then mirror horizontally
rules: 90° **clockwise** = transpose, then **reverse each row**. 90° counter-clockwise = transpose, then reverse each *column* (or reverse rows first).
Transpose with the inner loop starting at `j = i + 1`, not `j = 0` — touching the lower triangle too swaps every pair **twice** and undoes the transpose.
It must be **in place**: mutate the input matrix, don't return a new one. Returning a copy is the trap the prompt is built to catch.
The matrix is **square** (n×n). The transpose trick relies on that; a non-square matrix can't be rotated in place into the same buffer.
Derive the index map `new[j][n−1−i] = old[i][j]` on the board first — it's how you prove the transpose+reverse identity instead of memorising it.
whenToUse: Square matrix, rotate / reflect / transpose by a fixed angle
Interviewer adds 'do it in place' or 'O(1) extra space'
Coordinates map to coordinates by a clean linear rule
You can express the transform as a composition of simpler reflections
antiSignals: Non-square matrix → can't rotate in place; allocate the rotated buffer
Rotation by an arbitrary angle (not a multiple of 90°) → this is image processing, not this trick
You're allowed O(n²) extra space and clarity matters more → just copy with the index map
You need to rotate a *list* or *string*, not a grid → that's array reversal, not transpose
remember.takeaway: Any 90° rotation decomposes into a transpose plus a reflection. Once you see rotations as compositions of reflections, the whole family — rotate clockwise, counter-clockwise, 180°, flip diagonally — becomes the same two-line move with the reversal swapped around.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manipulate 2D indices without getting lost, and whether you know the transpose+reverse decomposition that turns a scary-looking rotation into two trivial passes — in place.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Allocating a second matrix when the prompt says in place, or transposing over the full grid (j from 0) which swaps every pair twice and leaves the matrix unchanged.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive new[j][n−1−i] = old[i][j] out loud, then say 'that's exactly transpose followed by reversing each row' — showing you understand WHY the trick works, not that you memorised it.

problemStatement:
You are given an `n x n` 2D `matrix` representing an image. Rotate the image by **90 degrees (clockwise)**.

You have to rotate the image ***in place***, which means you have to modify the input 2D matrix directly. **Do not** allocate another 2D matrix and do the rotation.
constraints: Rotation must be performed in place
understanding: Take a square grid and turn it a quarter-turn to the right, mutating the same array. The element at row i, column j must end up at row j, column n−1−i. The whole challenge is doing that without a second grid to copy into.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the matrix guaranteed square?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, n×n. That's what makes the in-place transpose legal — a rectangular matrix would change shape when rotated.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Clockwise or counter-clockwise?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Clockwise here. Counter-clockwise just swaps the second step: transpose then reverse each column instead of each row.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does 'in place' really forbid a second matrix?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the prompt explicitly says do not allocate another 2D matrix. A copy-based solution is correct mathematically but fails the constraint that's the whole point of the problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can n be 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A 1×1 matrix is its own rotation — both the transpose and the reversal are no-ops, so the code must handle it without special-casing.

examples.explanation: The left column 1,4,7 becomes the top row 7,4,1. Every column read bottom-to-top becomes a row left-to-right.
Same rule on a 4×4: the leftmost column (5,2,13,15) rotates up to become the top row read in reverse (15,13,2,5).
A single cell rotates onto itself.

approaches.name: Copy Into a New Matrix (Index Map)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to anchor the index mapping — then note the prompt forbids the extra matrix, which motivates the in-place trick.
hints: Where does the element at (i, j) go after a 90° clockwise turn? Trace one corner — the top-left (0,0) ends up at the top-right.
Work out the formula: a clockwise rotation sends (row i, col j) to (row j, col n−1−i). Build a fresh matrix using that map.
Allocate result[n][n], write result[j][n−1−i] = matrix[i][j] for every cell, then (if you must mutate) copy result back into matrix.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every one of the n² cells is read once and written once → O(n²) time. The second matrix is n² cells → O(n²) space, which is exactly what the prompt forbids.
approaches.explanation:
Build the answer in a brand-new matrix using the closed-form coordinate map, then (if the signature mutates in place) copy it back. The whole approach hinges on one formula.

**Deriving the map is the real work.** Picture the top row sliding to the right edge: the element at `(0, 0)` lands at `(0, n−1)`, and `(0, 1)` lands at `(1, n−1)`. Generalising, the cell at `(i, j)` moves to `(j, n−1−i)`. Equivalently, the cell that *ends up* at `(r, c)` came from `(n−1−c, r)`. Pick one direction and write it consistently — mixing the two is the classic off-by-rotation bug.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** With a spare matrix there's no aliasing to worry about: every write goes to a clean cell, so you never clobber a value you still need to read. It's the version you can get correct under pressure, and stating it proves you understand the *target* of the rotation before you optimise the storage away.

**Why we don't ship it.** It allocates a second n×n grid — precisely the thing the problem bans. It's here to pin down the index map; the in-place approach reuses that same geometric insight while spending O(1) extra space.
approaches.insight: The entire rotation is captured by one line: `new[j][n−1−i] = old[i][j]`. Everything clever that follows is just a way to realise that same permutation of cells *without* a second buffer. Get this map right and the optimal version is a two-step reflection of it.

approaches.name: Transpose + Reverse Each Row (Optimal, In Place)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'a clockwise rotation IS a transpose followed by a horizontal mirror' — derive it, don't just recite it.
hints: A rotation feels hard, but reflections are easy and in place. Can you build the rotation out of two reflections?
Transpose the matrix (swap M[i][j] with M[j][i]) — that flips it across the main diagonal. Now compare to the target: what single extra reflection finishes the job?
After transposing, reverse each row left-to-right. Transpose + horizontal mirror = 90° clockwise. Both steps mutate the matrix directly, so no extra grid.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Transpose touches each of the ~n²/2 upper-triangle pairs once; reversing all rows is another n²/2 swaps. Total O(n²) time, and every swap is in place so O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Do the rotation as two in-place reflections. First transpose the matrix across its main diagonal, then reverse each row. The composition of those two reflections is exactly a 90° clockwise rotation.

**Why transpose-then-reverse equals a clockwise rotation.** Transposing sends `(i, j)` to `(j, i)` — a flip across the main diagonal. Reversing each row then sends `(j, i)` to `(j, n−1−i)`. Compose them and the cell at `(i, j)` lands at `(j, n−1−i)` — the very map we derived in the first approach. Two cheap, in-place reflections multiply out to the one expensive-looking rotation. (Counter-clockwise is the same idea: transpose, then reverse each *column*.)

**Why the transpose loop starts at `j = i + 1`.** The transpose swaps `M[i][j]` with `M[j][i]`. If the inner loop ran `j` from `0`, you'd hit each off-diagonal pair twice — once as `(i, j)` and again as `(j, i)` — and the second swap would put everything back, leaving the matrix unchanged. Starting `j` at `i + 1` visits each pair exactly once and skips the diagonal (where `i == j` and the swap is pointless). This is the single most common bug in the whole problem.

**Why it's strictly better.** It's the same O(n²) cell-touches as the copy approach, but with no second grid — O(1) extra space, satisfying the constraint that defines the problem. And it generalises: swap the reversal step and you get every other right-angle rotation for free.
approaches.insight: Rotations are intimidating; reflections are trivial. The trick is realising any 90° rotation factors into two reflections you *can* do in place — a diagonal flip (transpose) and an axis flip (row reverse). Decomposing a hard transform into a product of easy ones is a reusable problem-solving move, not a Rotate-Image-only gimmick.

pitfalls: Inner loop j from 0 instead of i+1 — swaps every pair twice and leaves the matrix unchanged.
Reversing each row for counter-clockwise — CCW needs reversing the rows' order (or each column) instead.
Reversing first then transposing — order matters; that produces a reflection, not a clean rotation.

commonMistakes: Allocating a second n×n matrix despite the explicit 'in place' constraint.
Transposing with the inner loop from j=0, which double-swaps every pair and undoes the transpose.
Confusing clockwise with counter-clockwise — reversing rows vs reversing columns after the transpose.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Transposing over the full grid (double swap)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Running the inner loop from j=0 swaps (i,j) and later (j,i) as well, so every off-diagonal pair is exchanged twice and ends up back where it started — the matrix looks untouched.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Mixing up clockwise and counter-clockwise
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Transpose-then-reverse-rows is clockwise. To go counter-clockwise you transpose then reverse the order of the rows (or reverse each column). Reversing the wrong axis silently produces the mirror of the intended rotation.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning a new matrix instead of mutating
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The signature returns void / None — the grader inspects the original object. Building and returning a fresh grid leaves the input untouched and fails even though the values are 'right'.
